title: Model Selection: Train / Validation / Test, multiple comparisons, and final training
overview: This lesson explains the model selection step in supervised machine learning: how to split data into training, validation and test sets, why we need both validation and test sets (the multiple-comparison / "lucky model" problem), how to run the selection loop across candidate models, and how to produce the final model by retraining on combined data. The notes include the algorithmic workflow, practical recommendations, a compact pseudocode example, and visual diagrams to aid understanding.

key_concepts.title: Model selection
key_concepts.description: The process of trying multiple candidate models and choosing the one that is expected to perform best on new, unseen data.
bullet_points: Train many different models (different algorithms or hyperparameters).
Compare their performance using a hold-out validation dataset (not used for training).
Select the best-performing model on the validation set.
Use a separate test set to confirm the selection was not due to chance.

key_concepts.title: Train / Validation / Test split
key_concepts.description: Partitioning the original labeled dataset into three non-overlapping subsets to support unbiased model selection and final evaluation.
bullet_points: Training set: used to fit model parameters (weights).
Validation set: used repeatedly during model selection for comparing models and tuning hyperparameters.
Test set: held out until the very end to get an unbiased estimate of how the selected model will perform in production.
Split ratios are flexible (common choices: 60/20/20, 70/15/15, etc.).

key_concepts.title: Multiple comparison ("lucky model") problem
key_concepts.description: When evaluating many models on the same validation set, one model may achieve high validation performance purely by chance.
bullet_points: Randomness in training (initialization, stochastic optimization) or in model structure can produce a model that fits the validation set by luck.
Selecting the model with the highest validation score without further checks can lead to an over-optimistic estimate.
A held-out test set is required to verify that the selected model's performance generalizes.

key_concepts.title: Final training on combined data
key_concepts.description: After model selection and verification on the test set, you can (optionally) retrain the chosen model using both training and validation data to leverage more labeled data for the final production model.
bullet_points: Combining train + validation increases the amount of data used for fitting final model parameters.
Retrain only after model architecture/hyperparameters are finalized (i.e., after test verification).
Do not use the test set for training; test remains reserved for final evaluation.

key_concepts.title: Practical measures and tradeoffs
key_concepts.description: Operational considerations when implementing model selection in practice.
bullet_points: Stratify splits when the target class distribution is imbalanced.
Use cross-validation for small datasets instead of a single validation split (reduces variance).
Monitor metrics beyond accuracy: precision/recall, AUC, calibration, depending on problem.
Be mindful of leaking information from test into training (data leakage).

blocks.content: When you deploy a model you use a model trained on past data to predict on future examples. To estimate how the model will behave after deployment, simulate this by removing a slice of your dataset and treating it as unseen data (validation). Training should only use the remaining portion.

items: Split data into 'seen' (train) and 'unseen' (validation) portions.
Train model only on training set (features X_train, labels y_train).
Apply trained model to X_val and compare predictions to y_val.
Metrics computed on validation act as proxies for future performance.

detailed_explanations.title: Converting probabilities to predictions and computing metrics

blocks.content: Many classifiers output probabilities (e.g., probability spam = 0.7). Convert probabilities to class labels using a threshold (often 0.5) to compute discrete metrics like accuracy. Alternatively, evaluate metrics that use probabilities directly (AUC, log-loss) when more informative.

items: Probabilities: continuous outputs (e.g., 0.8, 0.6, 0.1).
Thresholding: label = 1 if prob >= threshold else 0 (default threshold 0.5).
Classification accuracy = fraction of correct label predictions on validation set.
When class imbalance exists, prefer precision/recall/F1 over raw accuracy.

detailed_explanations.title: Multiple comparisons — the coin flip example (why test set needed)

blocks.content: If you evaluate many candidate models on one fixed validation set, purely random models (a coin flip classifier) can sometimes match the validation labels perfectly by chance. This causes false confidence that a model generalizes. The test set is an independent check to detect lucky validation results.

items: Example: several random models evaluated on the same 20% validation subset — one may by chance achieve very high accuracy on that subset.
Selecting the model with highest validation performance risks choosing a 'lucky' model.
A separate test set guards against this by providing an out-of-selection check.

blocks.diagram:
flowchart TD
  A[Full labeled dataset] --> B[Split: Train / Val / Test]
  B --> C[Train candidate models on Train]
  C --> D[Evaluate each model on Val]
  D --> E[Select best model by Val performance]
  E --> F[Confirm selected model on Test]
  F --> G{If Test ok?}
  G -- Yes --> H[Optionally retrain chosen model on Train+Val and deploy]
  G -- No --> I[Revisit modeling choices / collect more data / change features]

items: 1) Split dataset into three non-overlapping parts (Train / Validation / Test).
2) Train models on the training set only.
3) Evaluate models on the validation set and compare metrics.
4) Select the best model based on validation performance.
5) Evaluate the selected model once on the test set to verify it wasn't lucky.
6) Optionally retrain the chosen model on Train + Validation, then use that as the production model; test remains reserved for final confirmation.

detailed_explanations.title: Pseudocode: implement a simple model selection loop

blocks.code:
# High-level pseudocode for model selection
# Assumes candidate_models is a list of initialized model objects
# split_dataset returns (X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test)
X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test = split_dataset(data, ratios=(0.6,0.2,0.2))
results = []
for model in candidate_models:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)            # train only on training set
    probs = model.predict_proba(X_val)     # or model.predict for deterministic models
    preds = (probs[:,1] >= 0.5).astype(int)  # threshold at 0.5
    score = accuracy(y_val, preds)         # or another metric
    results.append((model, score))

# Select best model by validation score
best_model, best_score = max(results, key=lambda x: x[1])

# Confirm with test set
probs_test = best_model.predict_proba(X_test)
preds_test = (probs_test[:,1] >= 0.5).astype(int)
test_score = accuracy(y_test, preds_test)
print('Validation score:', best_score)
print('Test score:', test_score)

# Optional: retrain best model on Train + Val for final deployment
best_model.fit(concat(X_train, X_val), concat(y_train, y_val))
# Save or deploy best_model

items: Do not use the test set during model selection or hyperparameter tuning — it must be held out until the final confirmation.
If your dataset is small, use cross-validation on training data for robust model comparison; still keep a final test set if possible.
Stratify splits to preserve class proportions across train/val/test for classification problems.
If you iterate on the validation set repeatedly (multiple rounds of selection), be aware you implicitly tune to validation — consider nested cross-validation or reserving a fresh test set.
Choose evaluation metrics aligned with business goals (accuracy is not always appropriate).
Random seeds and reproducibility: set fixed seeds for deterministic splits when you need repeatable experiments.

key_takeaway: Always split your labeled data into at least three parts: train, validation, and test.
Use the validation set to compare and select models; use the test set only once to confirm the selection.
Multiple candidate evaluations can produce a 'lucky' model—the test set guards against this risk.
After selection and test verification, you can retrain the final model on train+validation to maximize training data before deployment.
project_ideas: Implement a model-selection pipeline that compares several classifiers and reports validation/test metrics; include stratified splits and optional retraining on train+val.
Create an experiment to demonstrate the multiple-comparison problem: evaluate many random classifiers on the same validation split and show variance in validation vs test performance.
Build a small toolkit that automates train/validation/test splitting, metric calculation, and final retraining, with configuration for split ratios and random seeds.
